title: City money that the return does not show as government money
question: Where the City's payments fit inside total revenue, do they also fit inside the lines where a return reports government grants and fees for services?
finding: 33 organizations had at least one year in which the City paid $250,000 or more and that sum was larger than the government grants and programme fees on the return put together, by at least a tenth; 13 of them left the government-grants line blank or at zero in the year shown. The largest difference is at Five Keys Schools And Programs: $54.3 million paid by the City in the tax year ended 30 June 2025, against $44.9 million of government grants and $0 of programme fees reported. Years already listed in the first screen are left out.
how: Same alignment and pooling rule as the first screen. The City's payments in the tax year are compared with the sum of two lines of the return: government grants (Part VIII line 1e) and programme service revenue (fees and contracts for services, line 2g). Listed when City payments are at least $250,000 and exceed that sum by $100,000 and 10% of the City amount. One row per organization, largest difference first.
limits: This is a question of labelling more than of money. Preparers differ on where a City contract belongs, and some enter all grants on the line for other gifts. A parent or fiscal sponsor may be paid for a project that reports elsewhere. What the pattern does mean is that a reader of the return cannot see how far the organization depends on public money. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. For 23 of the 485 organizations matched here that makes the City figure at least $1 million and 10% higher over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $1.36 billion higher in all. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. A return may not count money that passes through as revenue. For the organizations matched here, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $425.1 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (14 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. Organizations are matched to tax returns by payee name and employer number; a wrong match would create a false gap.
